title: ossl-fuku-transfer
text: This project studies how well CNN models of soil mid-infrared (MIR) spectra transfer from the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), measured on Bruker instruments, to soil spectra from Fukushima, measured on a Thermo Nicolet. A model can reach state-of-the-art accuracy on OSSL and still fail on spectra from another spectrometer. This project measures how large that gap is, and what causes it.

title: ossl-fuku-transfer
text:
Questions

Zero-shot transfer: how well does a model trained on OSSL predict exchangeable potassium (Kex), cation exchange capacity (CEC) and organic carbon for the Fukushima samples, with no fine-tuning?
Cause of the gap: similar losses across properties point to the instrument, for example baseline or scatter. Different losses point to specific bands or to the soil population. A PCA fitted on OSSL compares the Fukushima spectra with KSSL Andisols and with the rest of KSSL.
Fine-tuning: how many Fukushima samples does a pretrained model need to reach a given R², compared with a model trained on Fukushima samples only?

title: ossl-fuku-transfer
text:
Set-up
The project uses the soilspec packages (soilspecdl, soilspecdata and soilspectfm) as editable installs from sibling folders:
soilspec/
  ossl-fuku-transfer/
  soilspecdl/
  soilspecdata/
  soilspectfm/
Clone the four repositories into one folder, then, in ossl-fuku-transfer/:
uv sync --extra dev
The Fukushima data is not public. This repository does not contain it. With access to it, put it in data/fukushima/ in the workspace folder, beside the project folders, or set SOILSPEC_DATA to the folder that holds fukushima/. nbdev-test skips the cells that read the data. Run nbdev-test --flags fukudata to include them.

pretrain splits OSSL at random into 90% training and 10% validation, and trains for epochs one-cycle epochs, as in the soilspecdl quick start. It saves the weights and the training history in model_dir(). A later call with the same fname loads them instead of training again. Delete the files to train again. Training on an Apple silicon GPU (MPS) is not fully deterministic, even with a fixed seed.

    y, # Targets, as passed to `pretrain`

A model scored over a narrow range has a lower R² than over a wide one, because the targets vary less. range_check measures a pretrained model on the part of its OSSL validation set that covers the Fukushima range. This gives the reference for Fukushima results.

predict
def predict(
    model, # Trained model
    X, # Preprocessed spectra, one per row
    bs:int=256, # Batch size
)->numpy.ndarray: # One prediction per spectrum
Predict X with model, applying BatchSNV to each spectrum first, as in training


predict gives the same predictions as test_preds for the same model and spectra:

m_syn = new_model()
test_close(predict(m_syn, X_syn[is_test_syn]), test_preds(spectral_learner(dls_syn, m_syn)), eps=1e-4)




adabn
def adabn(
    model, # Model returned by `pretrain`
    dls, # `DataLoaders` from `fuku_dls`
):
Copy of model whose BatchNorm running statistics are recomputed from the training and validation spectra of dls


BatchNorm layers normalize with running means and variances learned during training. A pretrained model keeps the OSSL statistics. On Fukushima spectra, whose distribution differs, each layer then receives off-center inputs. adabn (adaptive batch normalization) resets the statistics and recomputes them from every Fukushima spectrum outside the test set. Each running statistic becomes the average of the per-batch statistics, with every batch weighted equally. adabn changes no weights and uses no targets. Afterwards, the running mean of the first BatchNorm layer is the average over batches of the mean of the first convolution’s outputs:

m_ada = adabn(new_model(), dls_syn)
conv, bn = m_ada.backbone.layers[0].conv[0], m_ada.backbone.layers[0].conv[1]
with torch.no_grad(): outs = [conv(xb) for dl in (dls_syn.train.new(shuffle=False, drop_last=False), dls_syn.valid) for xb, _ in dl]
with torch.no_grad(): test_close(bn.running_mean.cpu().numpy(), torch.stack([o.mean(dim=(0, 2)) for o in outs]).mean(0).cpu().numpy(), eps=1e-6)




fit_models
def fit_models(
    pretrained, # Model returned by `pretrain`
    X, # Preprocessed Fukushima spectra
    y, # Targets
    is_test, # True for the samples of the fixed test set
    seed:int=0, # Seed for the validation split and the training
    epochs:int=20, # Training epochs after the first, frozen, epoch of fine-tuning
    lr:float=0.001, # Maximum learning rate
    schedules:NoneType=None, # Model name: (epochs, maximum learning rate), for 'fully fine-tuned' and 'Fukushima only'
)->dict: # Model name: test predictions
Test predictions of the models in model_names


The six models see the same validation split. The trained models see the same number of epochs:

Zero-shot predicts with the pretrained model as it is.
Zero-shot AdaBN predicts with the pretrained model after adabn has recomputed its BatchNorm statistics on the non-test Fukushima spectra. It uses no Fukushima targets.
Head only trains the pretrained head, a linear layer of 257 weights, for epochs + 1 epochs. The backbone weights stay fixed, including the BatchNorm scale and shift. The BatchNorm running statistics still update to the Fukushima batches during training.
Fine-tuned uses fastai’s fine_tune: one epoch with the backbone frozen at learning rate lr, then epochs epochs of the whole model. In that second phase the head’s maximum learning rate is lr / 2, and the backbone’s is lr / 200. With lr=1e-3, the backbone trains at most at 5e-6, 200 times lower than the Fukushima-only model, and stays close to its pretrained weights.
Fully fine-tuned trains the whole pretrained model with the schedule of the Fukushima-only model: epochs + 1 one-cycle epochs at maximum learning rate lr. It differs from the Fukushima-only model only in its starting weights.
Fukushima only trains new_model from random weights for epochs + 1 epochs.

schedules gives the fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models their own number of one-cycle epochs and maximum learning rate, such as ones chosen with cv_curves and cv_final below. Without it, both use the defaults above.
With an untrained model in place of a pretrained one and one epoch, each model predicts the 20 test samples:

preds_syn = fit_models(new_model(), X_syn, y_syn, is_test_syn, epochs=1)
test_eq({k: v.shape for k, v in preds_syn.items()}, {k: (20,) for k in model_names})

    p, # Predicted targets

A prediction that adds a constant to every log1p target keeps a correlation of 1, but loses R², and gains a bias:

test_close(s['r'], 1)

Choosing a schedule
The schedules of the fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models are chosen on the Fukushima training samples only. The test set plays no part in the choice. fuku_lr_find runs fastai’s learning rate finder from the pretrained weights, or from random weights when model is None:

    show_plot:bool=True, # Plot the loss against the learning rate

Run lr_find on the Fukushima training samples

cv_final
def cv_final(
    res:pandas.DataFrame
)->dict: # Mean and standard deviation over folds
Validation loss and R² at the last epoch of cv_curves, as mean and standard deviation over folds





cv_curves
def cv_curves(
    model, # Model returned by `pretrain`, or None for random weights
    X, # Preprocessed Fukushima spectra
    y, # Targets
    is_test, # True for the samples of the fixed test set
    lr, # Maximum learning rate
    epochs, # Number of one-cycle epochs
    fname:NoneType=None, # File name to cache the results under, without extension
    n_splits:int=5, # Number of folds
    seed:int=42, # Seed for the folds
)->pandas.DataFrame: # One row per fold and epoch, from `cross_validate`
Cross-validate one-cycle training on the Fukushima training samples


cv_curves trains one model per fold on the training samples, and records the losses and R² after every epoch. plot_cv from soilspecdl plots them. Results are cached under fname in model_dir(), so a notebook rerun does not repeat the training. cv_final summarises the last epoch, which is the one a one-cycle schedule ends on. On random data, R² stays near 0 or below:

res_cv = cv_curves(None, X_syn, y_syn, is_test_syn, lr=1e-3, epochs=2, n_splits=2)
test_eq(len(res_cv), 2 * 2)
{k: round(v, 3) for k, v in cv_final(res_cv).items()}

title: CEC
text:
Findings
The pretrained model comes from one pretraining run. The Fukushima-side training was repeated with five seeds. Training on MPS is not fully deterministic, and the variation between pretraining runs is not measured. All results use SNV followed by the first derivative.
Cross-validation on the training samples chose a maximum learning rate of 3e-3 for both the fully fine-tuned and the Fukushima-only model, the highest rate tried. It chose 40 epochs for the fully fine-tuned model and 80 for the Fukushima-only model, the longest run tried. Both choices for the Fukushima-only model are at the edge of the grid, so it may improve further. In cross-validation, the two models reached about the same validation R²: 0.75 for both, with standard deviations over the folds of 0.03 to 0.04.
With these schedules, the fully fine-tuned model is slightly better on the test set: an R² of log1p(CEC) of 0.74, a correlation of 0.86 and an RMSE of 2.8 cmolc/kg, against 0.71, 0.85 and 2.9 cmolc/kg for the Fukushima-only model. The standard deviations over the seeds are 0.004 and 0.014 in R². The standard deviation of the test CEC values is 5.6 cmolc/kg. Before tuning, with 21 epochs at 1e-3 for both models, the gap was much larger (0.72 against 0.59). Most of that gap came from undertraining the Fukushima-only model. The pretrained model needs half the epochs.
On OSSL validation samples within Fukushima’s CEC range (11.2 to 30.8 cmolc/kg), the pretrained model reaches an R² of 0.66 and a correlation of 0.86. Both tuned Fukushima models do about as well on the Fukushima test set.
The OSSL backbone does not work unchanged. Without training, it partly ranks the Fukushima samples (correlation 0.57) but predicts too low, with a bias of -3.0 cmolc/kg. A linear head on the frozen backbone gives an R² of 0.31, and fastai’s fine_tune, whose backbone trains at a maximum learning rate of 5e-6, gives 0.39. These models keep their default schedules.
Recomputing the BatchNorm statistics on the non-test Fukushima spectra (AdaBN) does not help. The zero-shot bias changes from -3.0 to +4.1 cmolc/kg, the R² stays near -0.65, and the correlation stays at 0.55. The failure to transfer lies in the features, not in the BatchNorm statistics.
The fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models have similar errors in each soil type, year and batch.

Each preprocessing is fitted on OSSL, then applied to the Fukushima spectra. The PCA, with 10 components, is fitted on OSSL only. T2 is Hotelling’s T², the distance within the PCA model. Q is the squared residual, the part of a spectrum the model does not explain:

pipes = {'SNV': make_pipeline(SNV()),
         'SNV + SG first derivative': make_pipeline(SNV(), SavitzkyGolay(window_length=11, polyorder=2, deriv=1))}

def fit_pca(pipe, n=10):
    Xo = pipe.fit_transform(om.spectra); Xf = pipe.transform(fuku.spectra)
    pca = PCA(n_components=n, svd_solver='randomized', random_state=0).fit(Xo)
    To, Tf = pca.transform(Xo), pca.transform(Xf)
    Eo, Ef = Xo - pca.inverse_transform(To), Xf - pca.inverse_transform(Tf)
    t2 = lambda T: (T**2 / pca.explained_variance_).sum(1)
    return dict(pca=pca, To=To, Tf=Tf, T2o=t2(To), T2f=t2(Tf), Qo=(Eo**2).sum(1), Qf=(Ef**2).sum(1), ro=(Eo**2).mean(0), rf=(Ef**2).mean(0))

title: OSSL and Fukushima spectra
text:
Findings
The figures in this section come from the tables above. They describe the current sample selection.
With SNV only, the Fukushima spectra sit away from OSSL. 22% of the Fukushima samples, and 41% of the Fukushima Andosols, are beyond the 99th percentile of OSSL’s T². The Fukushima Andosols are no closer to the OSSL Andisols than the other Fukushima soils are. Both Fukushima groups sit between 1.7 and 2.0 standard deviations below the OSSL mean on PC1, and between 2.5 and 2.8 below it on PC3. The OSSL Andisols sit at -0.75 on PC1 and +0.72 on PC3. The Andosols and the other Fukushima soils share the offset. This points to the instrument or to sample handling common to all Fukushima samples, more than to the soils.
The Savitzky-Golay first derivative removes most of the offset. No Fukushima sample is beyond OSSL’s 99th percentile of T², and 1.2% are beyond its 99th percentile of Q. An offset of about 1.5 standard deviations remains on PC2, against 0.2 for the OSSL Andisols. Most of the difference under SNV is therefore broad, such as baseline or slope.
The OSSL model leaves its largest Fukushima residuals between 3500 and 3950 cm⁻¹: 5.7 times the OSSL residual with SNV and 6.9 times with the derivative. In the quiet region from 2400 to 2800 cm⁻¹ the ratio is about 3.5. The narrow structure in 3500–3950 cm⁻¹ is not above that of the quiet region. The excess is a broad absorption, such as O–H from water held in the samples, more than water vapour lines.
Between 1300 and 2000 cm⁻¹, the Fukushima spectra have 2.1 times the narrow structure of OSSL, against 1.6 times in the quiet region. This excess is consistent with water vapour lines from the Nicolet’s beam path. The Fukushima spectra were interpolated linearly from a step of about 1.93 cm⁻¹ to 2 cm⁻¹, which smooths narrow lines a little. The narrow-structure ratios may therefore understate the Nicolet’s lines.
The CO₂ band is not a problem for Fukushima. Its spectra have less narrow structure there than OSSL (0.42 times), and the derivative model explains the band better for Fukushima than for OSSL.
The two Fukushima batches differ by about 0.8 standard deviations on PC3 with SNV. After the derivative their means differ by at most 0.12 standard deviations on each component. This notebook does not check whether the batches also differ in their soils.
Open questions for the Fukushima data team: how the samples were dried and stored before scanning, and whether the Nicolet was purged with dry air.

text:
Findings
The pretrained model comes from one pretraining run. The Fukushima-side training was repeated with five seeds. Training on MPS is not fully deterministic, and the variation between pretraining runs is not measured. All results use SNV followed by the first derivative.
Cross-validation on the training samples chose a maximum learning rate of 3e-3 for both the fully fine-tuned and the Fukushima-only model, the highest rate tried. It chose 20 epochs for the fully fine-tuned model and 40 for the Fukushima-only model. The best rate is at the edge of the grid, so a higher rate may do better. In cross-validation, the two models were close: a validation R² of 0.30 for the fully fine-tuned model and 0.27 for the Fukushima-only model, with standard deviations over the folds of 0.05 to 0.07.
With these schedules, the fully fine-tuned model is slightly better on the test set: an R² of log1p(Kex) of 0.41 and a correlation of 0.64, against 0.37 and 0.61 for the Fukushima-only model. The standard deviations over the seeds are 0.01 and 0.03. Before tuning, with 21 epochs at 1e-3 for both models, the gap was larger (0.37 against 0.30). Most of that gap came from undertraining the Fukushima-only model. The pretrained model needs half the epochs.
The best model has an RMSE of 0.31 cmolc/kg, against a standard deviation of 0.41 cmolc/kg for the test Kex values.
The OSSL backbone does not work unchanged. Zero-shot prediction fails (R² below 0, correlation 0.13). A linear head on the frozen backbone gives an R² of 0.11, and fastai’s fine_tune, whose backbone trains at a maximum learning rate of 5e-6, gives 0.09. These models keep their default schedules.
Recomputing the BatchNorm statistics on the non-test Fukushima spectra (AdaBN) removes most of the zero-shot bias, from +0.29 to +0.02 cmolc/kg. The R² rises from -0.82 to -0.15. The correlation barely changes, from 0.13 to 0.19. The OSSL BatchNorm statistics cause an offset, but the failure to rank the Fukushima samples lies in the features themselves.
The zero-shot failure is not explained by Fukushima’s narrower Kex range: on OSSL validation samples within that range, the pretrained model keeps a correlation of 0.73. Nor is it explained by the relation between Kex and the soil: the Spearman correlation of Kex with CEC is 0.29 in Fukushima and 0.33 in OSSL samples within the same range.
The fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models have similar errors in each soil type, year and batch.

text:
Findings
376 soils have both Bruker and Thermo spectra after the exclusions. 316 of them are Kazu samples, which are outside the sample selection of 03_kex and 04_cec. Which Bruker instrument and accessory measured them is not known yet.
The two instruments record the same soils at very different contrast. The Bruker spectra have a mean absorbance of 1.92 and a mean within-spectrum standard deviation of 0.40. The Thermo spectra have 0.51 and 0.066: about six times less contrast. SNV removes a difference of scale and offset, but not a non-linear one. Such a large difference in contrast suggests a difference in measurement mode or sample preparation, such as dilution, particle size or the accessory, more than a difference between spectrometers.
The spectral shapes of the same soil differ. The median correlation between a soil’s Bruker and Thermo spectra is 0.27 for raw and SNV spectra. After the first derivative it is 0.78, because the derivative removes the broad baseline differences.
Across soils, the instruments disagree most between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹, the region of the Si–O bands of quartz and clay minerals. There, the correlation between instruments over the soils is 0.10 with SNV and 0.43 with the derivative. In the water bands, 1300–2000 and 3500–3950 cm⁻¹, it is about 0.6. In diffuse reflectance, the bands in this mineral region are the most sensitive to particle size and dilution.
Wavenumber calibration and resolution are minor. The best alignment shifts the Thermo bands by 1.6 cm⁻¹ and raises the correlation of the mean derivative spectra from 0.805 to 0.809. Smoothing the Bruker spectra by a Gaussian of up to 6 cm⁻¹ lowers the derivative mismatch by about 10%. Smoothing the Thermo spectra lowers it by about 3%. The Bruker bands are slightly narrower.
In a PCA fitted on OSSL, both instruments’ spectra of these soils sit within OSSL’s 99th percentiles of T² and Q. The Thermo spectra sit further from the OSSL mean on PC2: -1.40 standard deviations, against -1.01 for the Bruker spectra.
The OSSL models transfer better from the Bruker spectra, but not well. For CEC, zero-shot prediction from the Bruker spectra gives a correlation of 0.66 and an R² of 0.24. From the Thermo spectra of the same soils it gives 0.53 and -0.51. The bias is +2.0 cmolc/kg from Bruker and +5.1 from Thermo. For Kex, both instruments fail (correlation 0.19 and 0.15). The instrument explains part of the CEC gap. The rest, and most of the Kex gap, comes from these soils or their preparation, which OSSL does not cover, or from the Bruker instrument differing from the instruments behind OSSL.
Questions for the Fukushima data team follow from this: the accessory of each instrument, whether the samples were diluted (for example with KBr) or measured neat, and how finely they were ground.
